# Scope and Lifetime {.unnumbered}

**Scope** = where the name can be used. **Lifetime** = how long the storage exists. Different questions.

## The table

| Declared | Scope | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|
| in a block `{ }` | that block, from the declaration down | until the block ends |
| function parameter | the function body | until it returns |
| outside all functions | every function below it in the file | whole program |
| outside all functions, `static` | the same, **but no other file can reach it** | whole program |
| in a block, `static` | that block only | **whole program** |

`static` inside a function changes the **lifetime**, not the scope. For `static`, `extern`, `register` and `auto` in full, see [Storage classes](storage-classes.qmd).

## One program, all of it

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int g = 1;                    /* global: whole program            */
static int fileOnly = 2;      /* global, this file only           */

void counter(void){
    static int calls = 0;     /* keeps its value between calls    */
    int fresh = 0;            /* new every call                   */
    calls++; fresh++;
    printf("  calls=%d fresh=%d\n", calls, fresh);
}

int main(void){
    int x = 10;
    printf("g=%d fileOnly=%d x=%d\n", g, fileOnly, x);
    {
        int x = 20;           /* shadows the outer x in this block */
        printf("inner block x=%d\n", x);
    }
    printf("after the block x=%d\n", x);
    counter(); counter(); counter();
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { int t = i * 10; printf("  loop i=%d t=%d\n", i, t); }
    return 0;
}
```

```
g=1 fileOnly=2 x=10
inner block x=20
after the block x=10
  calls=1 fresh=1
  calls=2 fresh=1
  calls=3 fresh=1
  loop i=0 t=0
  loop i=1 t=10
```

| In that output | Because |
|---|---|
| inner `x` is 20, outer still 10 | the inner `int x` is a **second** variable — shadowing |
| `calls` = 1, 2, 3 | `static` — storage survives the return, initialised once |
| `fresh` = 1 every time | ordinary local — created and destroyed each call |
| `i`, `t` | scoped to the loop; using them after it is an error |

## Parameters are copies

```c
void addOne(int n)        { n = n + 1; }     /* changes the copy only */
void reallyAddOne(int *n) { *n = *n + 1; }   /* changes the caller's  */
```

(Two different names — defining `addOne` twice is an error.)

## Traps

| | |
|---|---|
| accidental shadowing | legal, silent; a value "not changing" is often a shadow |
| block variable used after the block | `undeclared identifier` — the declaration is inside braces it should be outside |
| returning `&local` | undefined behaviour; storage is gone, may appear to work |
| globals as a shortcut | anything can change them, nothing records what did |

## Rules of thumb

**1. Declare a variable in the smallest block that needs it.**

If a variable is only used inside a loop, declare it inside the loop. The compiler then
refuses to let you use it anywhere else, which turns a whole class of mistake into an error
you see immediately instead of a wrong answer you have to hunt for.

```c
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {    /* i belongs to the loop        */
    int doubled = a[i] * 2;      /* doubled belongs to one pass  */
    total += doubled;
}
/* using i or doubled here is an error — which is the point */
```

It also keeps the reader's job small: a name declared three lines above is one you can still
see, and one declared at the top of a 60-line function is not.

**2. If the same name appears in nested scopes, rename one of them.**

The inner declaration *shadows* the outer one: both exist, and the name refers to whichever
is nearer. This is legal, so the compiler says nothing, and the symptom is a value that
"refuses to change".

```c
int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    int count = 0;        /* a SECOND count — the outer one never moves */
    count++;
}
printf("%d\n", count);    /* prints 0, not n */
```

Rename the inner one (`seen`, `local`, anything) and the bug cannot occur. Note this applies
to function parameters too: a parameter named `count` shadows a global `count` for the whole
function body.

`-Wall -Wextra` does **not** warn about this. The flag that does is `-Wshadow`, and it is not
switched on by default:

```
warning: declaration shadows a local variable [-Wshadow]
```

**3. Use a `static` local only when a value genuinely must survive between calls.**

The legitimate cases are narrow — counting how many times a function has run, remembering a
result that is expensive to recompute, holding a one-time setup flag.

```c
void logLine(char s[]) {
    static int lineNo = 0;       /* survives; numbers the output */
    lineNo++;
    printf("%d: %s\n", lineNo, s);
}
```

The cost is that the function is no longer predictable from its arguments alone: calling it
twice with the same input gives different output. That makes it harder to test and harder to
reason about, so it should be a decision, not a convenience. If the caller could just as
easily pass the value in and get it back, do that instead.

**4. Avoid globals in this course — pass values in and return them out.**

A global is in scope for every function below it, so any of them can change it and nothing
records which one did. When the value is wrong you have no shortlist of suspects, and the
function's signature no longer tells you what it depends on.

```c
int total;                    /* global */
void addTo(int x) { total += x; }     /* what else touches total? you must read everything */

int addTo(int total, int x) { return total + x; }   /* better: it is all in the signature */
```

The exception is a genuine program-wide constant, and for that prefer `#define MAX 100` or
`const`, which cannot be modified by accident.
